title: MCP Goes Stateless, and Developers Ask Whether That Just Makes It an API Again
gist: The MCP 2026-07-28 spec drops protocol sessions and adds two mandatory headers (Mcp-Method, Mcp-Name) that let gateways, rate limiters and WAFs route, throttle and meter agent traffic without parsing the JSON-RPC body — moving agent governance from a separate control layer into the transport itself. The article's under-covered angle is that this makes MCP operationally indistinguishable from REST, and that the economics favor gateways, registries and auth layers over MCP servers themselves.

themes.theme: Headers turn MCP into governable infrastructure

insights.claim: The MCP 2026-07-28 specification makes two headers mandatory on Streamable HTTP requests — Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name — so a tool call arrives as Mcp-Method: tools/call with Mcp-Name: search, exposing request intent outside the JSON-RPC body.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Any existing API gateway, rate limiter or WAF can now govern agent traffic per method and per tool with no MCP-specific parsing — a step-change in deployability for enterprise agent stacks.
insights.quote: Two headers are now mandatory on Streamable HTTP requests: Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name.

insights.claim: Cloudflare's Matt Carey argues the new MCP headers let a gateway, rate limiter or WAF act per method and per tool using the same primitives already applied to every other API, rather than requiring body inspection.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Cloudflare is positioning its edge as the natural enforcement point for agent traffic — watch whether MCP governance becomes a monetized edge SKU.
insights.locator: Cloudflare's Matt Carey spells out what that buys you

insights.claim: Agent governance has until now been bolted on above the protocol as a separate control layer — Cloudflare's agent tracing and the AI Gateway tier of Azure API Management both sit above MCP — whereas this release puts the metadata into the transport where existing infrastructure can read it.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Products whose differentiation was 'we can parse MCP for you' lose that moat; the value shifts to policy, identity and metering rather than protocol comprehension.
insights.locator: Agent governance has been arriving from the other direction

insights.claim: The spec permits copying tool arguments into HTTP headers for custom routing, extending gateway-level control beyond method and tool name to argument-based traffic steering.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Argument-level routing enables tiering, cost-based routing and per-argument rate limits — the primitives needed to build a metered agent-traffic business.
insights.quote: tool arguments can be copied into headers for custom routing
insights.locator: Commenter evalstate noted the spec goes further

insights.claim: Earlier MCP transports required an initialize/initialized handshake tracked via an Mcp-Session-Id header, which pinned clients to whichever instance held their session and made load balancing impractical while forcing autoscaling infrastructure to preserve, drain or migrate sessions.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Quantifies why early MCP server deployments were expensive to run — the operational tax, not the protocol, was the adoption bottleneck.
insights.locator: Earlier transports opened with an initialize

insights.claim: Under the new protocol each request carries its own protocol version, client identity and capabilities, so any request can land on any instance — enabling commodity load balancing, progressive rollouts and standard autoscaling for MCP servers.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Removes the main infrastructure objection to running MCP servers at scale; expect a step-up in production MCP deployments and in serverless/edge hosting of them.
insights.quote: Any request can land on any instance.
insights.locator: The new protocol removes the handshake

insights.claim: Elicitation is the casualty of statelessness: server-initiated requests now use Multi Round-Trip Requests where the server returns input_required, the client collects the answer and retries, so a human approval becomes two requests instead of one held connection.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Simpler to deploy but the human wait no longer sits inside a single invocation — agent frameworks relying on blocking approval flows need rearchitecting.
insights.quote: Approval becomes two requests instead of one held connection, which is simpler to deploy but means the wait for a human no longer sits inside a single invocation.

insights.claim: MCP authorization tightened in the same release: Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated and slated for removal after summer 2027, RFC 9207 issuer identification is adopted, and clients must send the canonical server URI as the RFC 8707 resource so tokens are accepted only by that audience.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A hard deprecation deadline (post-summer 2027) creates a dated migration obligation for anyone shipping MCP clients today.

themes.theme: Is MCP just REST with a blessing?

insights.claim: A significant camp argues stateful MCP was clearly a mistake and that the stateless release reduces MCP to another REST API endpoint runnable on existing load balancers, API gateways and progressive rollout infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: If MCP is operationally REST, its defensibility rests entirely on ecosystem convention — a fragile moat that a competing blessed standard could take.
insights.quote: In retrospect, stateful MCP was clearly wrong. This essentially makes MCP just another REST API endpoint, and lets you use the same infrastructure you already have set up for REST APIs
insights.locator: For one camp, the release confirms

insights.claim: Critics frame stateless MCP as the industry relearning the Sun RPC lesson that stateless servers are always better and stateful ones justified only when unavoidable — a cycle of inventing state, discovering it does not scale, and arriving back at a POST request.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A pattern-recognition heuristic: new AI protocols that introduce server-side session state should be assumed to face the same forced simplification within ~2 years.
insights.quote: we invented a stateful protocol, discovered state is hard to scale, stripped it out, and arrived at "just send a POST request." the REST crowd has been smugly waiting for this moment for 20 years.

insights.claim: The structural critique of MCP decomposes it into a REST-like API, plus a spec of the kind OpenAPI already provides, plus harness-level authorization — arguing only the third component is genuinely new.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Isolates harness-level authorization as the only novel primitive — that is where any durable MCP-specific product value should be sought.
insights.locator: Commenter bloppe made the structural version

insights.claim: MCP's defenders concede the technical resemblance to JSON-RPC and REST but locate its value in distribution: it is a standard blessed by AI providers, which gave implementers strong incentives to actually adopt it, and a convention models were already trained to use.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The moat is coordination and model training data, not protocol design — meaning whoever the frontier labs bless controls the interface layer.
insights.quote: The core advantage MCP gave you was a standard that by virtue of being blessed by AI providers people had strong incentives to actually implement.
insights.locator: Commenter vidarh put the case most economically

insights.claim: David Cramer, co-founder and chief product officer at Sentry, who had previously written publicly that MCP was not yet good, says this release cleans up auth and tool handling, arguing agents only become useful once the plumbing stops being the whole story.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A previously public skeptic flipping is a meaningful sentiment marker for MCP's production-readiness inflection.
insights.quote: Agents only get useful once the plumbing stops being the whole story.
insights.locator: David Cramer, co-founder and chief product officer at Sentry

insights.claim: The argument that agents need shell access to ordinary CLI tools rather than a protocol assumes a developer on a laptop with a shell inside a coding harness, which describes a small fraction of usage versus the majority reached through phone apps, web chat and embedded widgets.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Distribution surface, not developer preference, decides the tool-access standard — bearish for CLI-first agent-tooling bets aimed at consumer-scale deployments.
insights.locator: A parallel thread questioned whether agents need a protocol

insights.claim: Anthropic reports MCP passed 400 million monthly SDK downloads, a fourfold increase this year, making protocol-level adoption the one point not in dispute across the debate.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A hard adoption number to anchor MCP ecosystem sizing — 4x YoY on SDK downloads is the growth rate to track for infrastructure demand.
insights.quote: Anthropic reports MCP passed 400 million monthly SDK downloads, a fourfold increase this year.

insights.claim: An audit of one client's MCP server found just 61 tool calls in three months, 58 of them from the client's own engineers, suggesting SDK download growth does not translate into usage at individual servers.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A sharp caution against extrapolating headline MCP adoption into demand for any given MCP server product; ask for tool-call volume, not download counts.
insights.quote: auditing a client's server that recorded 61 tool calls in three months, 58 of them from the client's own engineers

insights.claim: The money in the MCP ecosystem is flowing to gateways, registries and auth layers rather than to the MCP servers themselves — a claim made by a consultant who disclosed MCP work as a significant share of their own revenue.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Directs capital toward infrastructure chokepoints (Cloudflare, Azure API Management, registry/auth vendors) rather than toward MCP server builders.
insights.quote: The money is flowing to the gateways and registries and auth layers rather than to the servers themselves.
insights.locator: The author, who disclosed that MCP work

insights.claim: Teams running MCP in production face real migration work: servers relying on protocol sessions, server-to-client requests or standalone streams must run a stateless route beside the sessionful one, move features across, drain active sessions and remove the legacy path within the deprecation window, with updated TypeScript, Python, Go and C# SDKs available now.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Dual-path migration cost is a near-term drag on MCP server teams and a tailwind for tooling that automates the transition.
insights.locator: For teams already running MCP in production
